samples_judged.question_text: The school program begins in August and an exhibit happens in December. How many months later is the exhibit?
This month is October. What month will it be in 2 months?
A short break starts at 9:00 and lasts a quarter of an hour (15 minutes). What time does it end?
The clean-up time began at 9:00 and finished at 9:30. How many minutes did it last?
The school program begins in January and an exhibit happens in March. How many months later is the exhibit?
A short break starts at 11:00 and lasts a quarter of an hour (15 minutes). What time does it end?
Play time starts at 11:00 and lasts half an hour (30 minutes). What time does it end?
Look at the August 2025 calendar. What day of the week is August 30?
Morning exercise starts at 10:00 and lasts a quarter of an hour (15 minutes). What time does it end?
The recess began at 8:00 and finished at 8:30. How many minutes did it last?

verdicts.reasoning: The items pose situations that need working out rather than bare recall: counting August forward to December for 4 (seed 11) and finding the elapsed minutes between 9:00 and 9:30 (seed 57).
Time is the subject matter throughout — clock times with hour and minute hands in the ClockSet payloads (seeds 42, 57), and calendar dates and months (seed 103). No sample is about anything else.

Whole hours appear only as the given starting point (9:00, 10:00, 11:00, 8:00); no sample asks for a one-hour duration, and every clock drawn shows :15 or :30, so the pupil is never asked to read or produce an on-the-hour time.
verdicts.action_taken: Filed as a §6F CONTRADICTED finding, unedited. Whole hours appear only as given start times (9:00, 10:00, 11:00, 8:00) and every clock drawn reads :15 or :30, so a one-hour duration is never asked for or shown. Sampler gap, same shape as B01's denominators: the fix widens the duration sampler to include whole hours.

verdicts.reasoning: Seed 91 names it outright — "lasts half an hour (30 minutes)" from 11:00 — and seeds 57 and 127 ask for the 30-minute span between 9:00/9:30 and 8:00/8:30.
verdicts.content_note_from_attester: Seed 127 asks "How many minutes did it last?" (key 30) but attaches an interactive clock in set mode (is_read_only false, target_time 8:30); the pupil is asked for a count of minutes while the response widget sets a clock face, so the answer type and the input do not match. Seed 91 has the same set-mode clock already carrying target_time 11:30, the answer being asked for.

verdicts.reasoning: Three stems state a quarter-hour duration explicitly — "lasts a quarter of an hour (15 minutes)" starting at 9:00, 11:00 and 10:00 — and the keys are the corresponding :15 end times.
verdicts.content_note_from_attester: On seeds 42, 78 and 118 the read-only ClockSet already displays the answer (target_time 9:15, 11:15, 10:15 respectively, matching the key), so the pupil can read the end time off the clock without adding a quarter hour to the start time.

verdicts.reasoning: Seed 103 requires locating August 30 on a calendar with show_day_names true and naming its weekday, keyed Saturday, which is correct for 2025 — that is day-of-week work. It is the only sample of the seven-day cycle in the set; nothing asks how many days are in a week or what day follows another.
Three items move across the calendar year: August to December as 4 months (seed 11), October plus 2 months giving December (seed 23), and January to March as 2 (seed 64).
verdicts.content_note_from_attester: The Calendar visual contradicts the stem in all three: seed 11 speaks of August and December but draws month 9 (September); seed 23 says "This month is October" but draws month 2 (February); seed 64 spans January to March but draws month 2 alone. A single-month calendar also cannot represent a multi-month duration, so the drawn aid is at best useless and at worst misleading.
